  • Burritos — a large flour tortilla wrapped tightly around a filling, like a bundle
  • Quesadillas — a tortilla folded in half with cheese (and other fillings) inside, then heated until the cheese melts
  • Enchiladas — corn tortillas rolled around a filling and then covered in a sauce and baked
  • Wraps — using a large flour tortilla as a sandwich wrap, rolled around any filling
  • Fajitas — grilled meat and vegetables served with tortillas so you can roll your own
  • Tostadas — a corn tortilla that is fried or baked until it becomes hard and crispy, then topped with food
  • Tortilla chips — corn tortillas cut into triangles and fried or baked until crunchy; the chips you dip into salsa or guacamole

So a tortilla can be soft (used fresh) or crispy (when fried or baked). In its soft form, it wraps around food. In its crispy form, it becomes a chip or a hard shell.

In Spain (and among Spanish speakers in Europe), the word "tortilla" — or more fully, tortilla española (Spanish tortilla) — refers to something entirely different: a thick, round omelette made primarily from eggs and potatoes.

This dish looks nothing like the Mexican flatbread. Imagine a thick, golden, round cake — almost like a pie in shape — made by slowly cooking sliced potatoes in olive oil, then mixing them into beaten eggs, and cooking the whole thing in a pan. The result is a firm yet tender, savoury egg-and-potato dish that is sliced into wedges like a cake and eaten at any time of day. It is one of the most beloved and iconic dishes in Spanish food culture.

It is often compared to an Italian frittata (a thick baked omelette) in terms of texture and concept. It may also include onions, and sometimes other vegetables, though the classic version is simply eggs and potatoes.

The Spanish tortilla is eaten as a snack (tapa), a light meal, or even packed in a sandwich. It is served warm or at room temperature.
Why the Same Word for Two Different Things?

Both share the word "tortilla" because, in Spanish, tortilla is simply the diminutive of torta — meaning a small round flat thing (a "little cake" or "little round"). The Mexican one is a flat round bread, and the Spanish one is a flat round egg dish. Both are round and flat — and both cultures independently used the same word. Over time, they diverged into two very distinct foods.
Quick Summary to Lock It In

Mexican TortillaSpanish Tortilla
What it isThin, flat, round breadThick omelette with eggs and potatoes
Made fromCorn or wheat flourEggs, potatoes, olive oil
TextureSoft and flexible (or crispy when fried)Firm, dense, sliceable
Used forTacos, burritos, wraps, chipsEaten as a dish, tapa, or sandwich filling

The word tortilla refers to a flat, round food item — but what that item actually is depends entirely on context. In everyday English and in Mexican/American cuisine, it almost always means the thin flatbread used to make tacos, burritos, and wraps. In a Spanish cultural context, it refers to a thick potato-and-egg omelette. Knowing both meanings makes you fully equipped to understand and use this word correctly in any situation you encounter it.
14831:
"Tortuous" means full of twists and turns. Something tortuous does not go straight. It bends, winds, curves, loops, and doubles back — either physically in space, or figuratively in thought, language, or process.

Picture a snake moving across the ground. It doesn't travel in a straight line; it curves and weaves constantly. That image is the soul of this word. Anything that moves, develops, or is structured the way that snake moves — not directly, not simply, but with many turns and complications — can be called tortuous.

When used about something physical, tortuous simply describes a path, road, river, or passage that winds and bends rather than going straight.

A mountain road that zigzags up a steep slope is tortuous. A river that snakes across a valley in wide, looping curves is tortuous. A narrow alley that twists through an old city, never holding one direction for long, is tortuous. There is no moral judgment here — it is purely descriptive. It just means: this thing bends a lot.

"The hikers made their way along a tortuous trail that wound through the dense forest for miles before finally opening onto the hilltop."

This is where the word becomes truly rich and useful, because "tortuous" is used just as often — perhaps even more often — to describe things you cannot see or touch: arguments, processes, explanations, negotiations, paths to success, and so on.

When something abstract is called tortuous, it means it is needlessly complicated, indirect, hard to follow, or full of unnecessary detours. Instead of going from Point A to Point B in a clear, direct way, it meanders, circles back, introduces confusing detours, and generally refuses to be simple.

Consider a legal process that involves dozens of steps, constant delays, contradictory rules, and endless paperwork before you can reach any resolution. That process is tortuous — it twists and turns on itself instead of leading you cleanly toward an outcome.

Or consider a speaker who, when asked a simple question, gives an answer that goes off in five directions at once, introduces unrelated points, circles back to earlier ideas without resolving them, and leaves you more confused than when you started. Their reasoning is tortuous.

"After tortuous negotiations that lasted three years, the two countries finally agreed to a peace deal."

"She gave a tortuous explanation of why she was late — involving a missed bus, a wrong turn, a lost phone, and a sudden downpour — none of which quite added up."

"The bill had a tortuous journey through parliament, being amended, rejected, revised, and debated for over a decade before it finally became law."

When used literally about a road or river, tortuous is neutral — it is just a description of shape, carrying no blame or criticism.

But when used figuratively, tortuous almost always carries a negative or at least unflattering tone. It implies that something is more complicated than it needs to be, that it is difficult to navigate, and that a more direct path would have been preferable. A tortuous argument suggests the speaker either cannot think clearly or is deliberately being evasive. A tortuous bureaucratic process suggests a system that has become tangled in its own rules. A tortuous plot in a novel suggests one that is hard to follow rather than cleverly layered.

In short: tortuous figuratively = unnecessarily complex, confusingly indirect, hard to follow.
The most important distinction: tortuous vs. torturous

These two words look almost identical and are constantly mixed up, even by native speakers. Knowing the difference will serve you well.

Tortuous (the word you are learning) means full of twists and turns; winding; convoluted.

Torturous means involving or causing torture; extremely painful or agonizing.

The road through the mountains is tortuous (it winds and bends).
A root canal at the dentist might be torturous (extremely painful).

A useful way to keep them apart: torturous contains the word "torture" almost completely within it — tortureous. If you see the word "torture" hiding inside it, you know it means pain and suffering. Tortuous, without that "re," is about twists and turns, not pain.

That said, life does create situations where both words could apply to the same thing in different ways. A tortuous mountain drive (winding) might also be torturous (agonizing) for someone with severe car sickness. The words are different in meaning but a situation can warrant both.
A mental anchor to remember it

Think of a tortoise. A tortoise does not move in a straight line quickly — it wanders, it curves, it takes the long winding way around. The word "tortuous" shares a feel (though not an etymology — which you've asked me to skip) with that slow, meandering, winding quality. Any time something winds and twists and takes the long, complicated route instead of going straight — that is tortuous.
A final summary in one sentence

Tortuous describes anything — a road, a river, an argument, a process, an explanation — that is full of twists, bends, and complications instead of being direct and straightforward, and when used figuratively it almost always suggests that this complexity makes things difficult and frustrating to follow or navigate.
14832:
Torture is the deliberate act of inflicting severe pain — physical, psychological, or both — on a person who cannot freely escape or stop it, usually to achieve a specific goal. The key word here is deliberate. Torture is never accidental. Someone actively chooses to cause that suffering, and that intention is what makes torture what it is.

Torture is about total control. The person being tortured is powerless, and the one doing it exploits that powerlessness completely.
What Makes Something "Torture" and Not Just "Pain"

This is an important distinction. Not every painful experience is torture. Three things must be true at the same time:

The suffering must be severe — not mild discomfort or ordinary pain, but extreme, overwhelming distress that breaks a person down physically or mentally.

It must be intentional — someone is deliberately causing it, not by accident or negligence.

It must be done to someone who is under the torturer's control — meaning the victim cannot simply walk away. They are trapped, imprisoned, restrained, or otherwise helpless.

When all three of these are present together, you have torture.

Torture is almost always done for something. The most common reasons are:

To extract information or a confession. Governments, interrogators, or criminals may torture someone to force them to reveal secrets, give names, or confess to a crime — whether they are truly guilty or not.

To punish. Torture has historically been used as a form of brutal punishment, to make someone suffer for something they did or were accused of doing.

To intimidate or control. Torturing one person sends a message to others: obey, or this happens to you. Authoritarian regimes and criminal organizations have used torture this way for centuries.

To break someone's will. Sometimes the goal is not specific information but total submission — to destroy a person's resistance, identity, or sense of self so completely that they comply with whatever is demanded.

Physical torture targets the body. Examples include severe beating, burning, electrocution, suffocation, forced stress positions, starvation, and sleep deprivation. Sleep deprivation is particularly notable — while it sounds mild, extended sleep deprivation causes hallucinations, cognitive collapse, and intense suffering, making it a recognized form of torture.

Psychological torture (also called mental torture) targets the mind without necessarily touching the body. It includes prolonged isolation (locking someone in total solitude with no human contact), threats against a person's loved ones, forced witnessing of violence, humiliation, sensory deprivation (blindfolding and silencing someone for extended periods), and deliberate disorientation. Psychological torture can cause damage just as severe and lasting as physical torture — and sometimes more so, because the scars are invisible.

In practice, the two forms are frequently used together.

Torture is universally condemned and illegal under international law. The United Nations Convention Against Torture, which nearly every country in the world has signed, defines it and prohibits it absolutely — meaning there is no legal situation, not even war, not even a national emergency, where torture is permitted. It is classified as a crime against humanity when practiced systematically.

Despite this, torture has occurred and continues to occur in various parts of the world, often hidden from public view in secret detention facilities. The gap between what the law says and what actually happens is one of the central concerns of human rights organizations.

It is also worth knowing that evidence obtained through torture is widely considered unreliable, because people in extreme pain will say almost anything — true or false — to make the suffering stop. This is one of the practical arguments against it, alongside the fundamental moral one.

In ordinary conversation, people use "torture" loosely and informally to describe something deeply unpleasant — not literally painful, but mentally exhausting or unbearable. For example:

"Sitting through a three-hour meeting about nothing was pure torture."
"Waiting for exam results is absolute torture."
"Being forced to listen to that music for hours was torture."

In these cases, the speaker is using the word for dramatic emphasis. No actual suffering is occurring — they are simply borrowing the intensity of the word to express strong displeasure. This is a well-understood and widely accepted figurative use, but it is clearly different from the literal, serious meaning of the word.

"The report documented evidence of systematic torture in the country's prisons."
"Survivors of torture often carry deep psychological trauma for the rest of their lives."
"The use of torture, no matter the justification, is a violation of human rights."
"He refused to reveal the information even under torture."

If you had to carry one sentence in your memory, it would be this: Torture is the deliberate infliction of severe physical or mental suffering on a helpless person, used as a tool of power to extract, punish, or control. Everything else in this explanation is detail and context built around that core.
14833: To torture someone means to deliberately cause them severe, intense pain — whether physical or mental — usually over a period of time. The single most important word in understanding "torture" is deliberately. Torture is never accidental. The person doing it always intends to cause suffering. This deliberate intent is what separates torture from simply hurting someone by mistake.

In its most direct, literal sense, to torture means to inflict serious physical pain on a person — or sometimes an animal — on purpose. This is typically done to punish someone, to force them to confess, or to extract information from them.

"The soldiers tortured the prisoners to get information."
"He was tortured for days before anyone knew where he was."

The pain involved is never mild or moderate. It is intense, prolonged, and deliberately applied. That is what makes the word so heavy and serious.

This is probably the most commonly used meaning in everyday life. When something tortures you emotionally, it causes you deep mental anguish, distress, or worry — often for a long stretch of time. The idea here is that emotional suffering can be just as agonizing as physical pain.

"Guilt tortured him for years after the accident."
"The thought of losing her job tortured her every night."
"Stop torturing yourself over something that happened so long ago."

Notice that last example — you can torture yourself. This means you are putting yourself through intense mental distress, often by obsessing over a mistake, a fear, or a regret.
Meaning 3: Twisting or Distorting Something (The Figurative Sense)

When "torture" is applied not to a person but to a thing — like language, music, logic, or facts — it means to force that thing into an unnatural, distorted, or unrecognizable shape. The underlying image is the same: something is being pushed painfully far beyond its natural limits.

"He tortured the English language with his incomprehensible sentences."
"She tortured the melody so badly that no one recognized the song."
"The politician tortured the facts to make himself look innocent."

Here, the language, melody, or facts are being bent and twisted until they lose their original form — just like a body under physical torture.
Meaning 4: Something Extremely Unpleasant (Informal, Exaggerated Use)

In casual, everyday conversation, people use "torture" as a dramatic exaggeration to describe something that is simply very unpleasant, boring, or tedious — even when no real pain is involved.

"Sitting through that four-hour presentation was pure torture."
"He tortured us with his endless, pointless stories."

This is hyperbole — deliberate overstatement for effect. Native speakers use it to emphasize just how unbearable an experience felt. Context always makes it clear when the word is being used this way.

Torture is a transitive verb, which means it always needs an object — you must always torture someone or something. You cannot simply say "he tortures" and leave it there; you must say who or what is being tortured.

It follows regular verb patterns:

  • Past tense: "They tortured him for hours."
  • Present continuous: "She is torturing herself with worry."
  • Past participle: "He had been tortured for information."

"Tortured" as an adjective — When you describe someone as having a tortured soul, a tortured mind, or a tortured expression, you mean they are deeply troubled, internally suffering, or visibly in anguish. It suggests a person carrying a heavy, ongoing burden of pain or guilt.

"He was a tortured artist who could never find peace."
The Thread Running Through All Meanings

No matter which sense the word is used in, three qualities are always present:

Deliberateness — Torture is never an accident. There is always intent behind it.

Severity — The suffering, pain, or distortion is always extreme, never mild or insignificant.

Duration — There is almost always a sense of it going on for some time, not being a single, brief moment.

These three qualities are the soul of the word. Whenever you encounter "torture" used as a verb — in news, in literature, in conversation — ask yourself: is it deliberate? Is it severe? Does it go on? If the answer is yes to all three, the word is being used accurately.
14834:
"Toss" means to throw something — but with a very specific flavor. It is a light, casual, effortless throw, usually over a short distance. It is not a powerful, full-effort throw (that would be hurl or fling). Think of a friend lazily throwing you a set of keys across the room — that's a toss. Easy. Relaxed. Almost careless.

This core idea of lightness and ease runs through almost every meaning of the word.

1. To throw something casually and without much effort

This is the most everyday meaning.

  • She tossed her bag onto the chair when she got home.
  • He tossed me a bottle of water from across the kitchen.
  • Just toss your jacket on the bed.

Notice that in all of these, nobody is throwing hard or with precision. It's a relaxed, informal action.

2. To flip a coin to make a decision

When you "toss a coin," you throw it upward into the air, let it land, and whatever side faces up determines the outcome. This is a very standard and widely used phrase.

  • We couldn't agree on where to eat, so we tossed a coin.
  • Let's toss for it — heads or tails?

Related expressions:

  • "Toss up" — when used as a verb phrase, it means to flip a coin. But "a toss-up" (as a noun) means a situation where two outcomes are equally likely. "It's a toss-up whether she'll accept the offer or not."

3. To mix food by gently turning it over

In cooking, "toss" means to mix ingredients by lifting and turning them so everything is evenly coated or combined. You do this gently — not stirring hard, but loosely tumbling things together.

  • Toss the salad in the dressing before serving.
  • He tossed the pasta with olive oil, garlic, and herbs.
  • Toss the vegetables in the pan to coat them in the sauce.

This is exactly what a chef does when they shake a frying pan to flip and mix the food inside it. The motion is effortless and light — consistent with the core idea.

4. To throw something away / discard it

In informal, everyday speech — especially in American English — "toss" very commonly means to throw something in the bin, i.e., to discard it.

  • That milk has gone bad. Just toss it.
  • I tossed all the old newspapers.
  • Feel free to toss anything you don't need.

5. To move restlessly — or to be thrown around by an external force

A. To toss and turn
This is a very common phrase meaning to move around in bed restlessly because you cannot sleep. Your body keeps shifting from side to side.

  • I tossed and turned all night, worrying about the exam.
  • He looked exhausted — he'd been tossing and turning for hours.

B. To be tossed about by a force (like wind or water)
When something is thrown around by a powerful force — like waves, wind, or turbulence — we say it is "tossed."

  • The small boat was tossed violently by the waves.
  • The storm tossed the debris across the street.

Here, it's not a person doing the tossing — nature or some external force is. But the image is the same: something being thrown around lightly and without control.

6. To toss one's head

This means to move your head in a quick, sharp motion — tilting it back or to the side. It is a body language gesture that usually signals annoyance, dismissal, pride, or flirtation, depending on the context.

  • She tossed her head and walked out of the room without a word. (dismissive, proud)
  • He tossed his head in the direction of the door, signaling me to leave. (a gesture/signal)

7. To search a place thoroughly (informal)

In informal usage, especially in American English, "toss" can mean to search a place intensively and messily — leaving it in disorder.

  • The police tossed his apartment looking for evidence.
  • Someone had tossed the office — drawers were open and papers were everywhere.

Toss out — to throw away or discard; also to suggest an idea informally.

  • We tossed out all the old furniture.
  • Let me toss out an idea and see what you think.

Toss off — to do or produce something very quickly and without much effort.

  • He tossed off the report in twenty minutes.
  • She tossed off a quick reply without really reading the message carefully.

Toss around / toss about — to discuss or consider ideas casually and loosely, without committing to anything.

  • We've been tossing around a few ideas for the new project.
  • The concept was tossed about in the meeting but nothing was decided.

The word "toss" almost always carries a feeling of ease, informality, and lack of precision. When you toss something, you are not being careful or deliberate. This is why:

  • You toss your keys on a table, but you place a fragile vase on a shelf.
  • You toss an idea into a conversation casually, but you present a formal proposal.
  • You toss a ball to a child in the garden, but a professional throws a pitch in a game.

Understanding this tone will help you use the word naturally in the right situations.

TossThrowFlingHurl
EffortLight, easyNeutralForceful, emotionalVery forceful
PrecisionLowModerateLowLow
FeelingCasualNeutralImpulsiveAggressive

For example:

  • He tossed the ball gently to the toddler.
  • He flung the ball in frustration when he missed.
  • He hurled the ball at the wall in a rage.

"Toss" as a verb means to throw something lightly and casually. This core image — of something being moved through the air effortlessly — stretches into cooking (mixing lightly), decision-making (flipping a coin), restless movement (tossing and turning), and informal speech (tossing an idea around). Whatever the specific situation, the feeling is always the same: light, easy, and without great care or precision.
14835: The word "tot" has two main meanings as a noun. Both share the idea of smallness at their core, but they are used in very different situations.

The most widely understood meaning of "tot" is a very small, young child — typically a toddler or infant. When someone calls a child a "tot," they are picturing a child who is small enough that they are just beginning to walk and talk, usually between about one and three years old.

The word is warm and affectionate in tone. It is not a clinical or official word. You would not use it in a medical report, but you would naturally use it when talking fondly about a child. For example, a grandparent watching a child take their first wobbly steps might say, "Look at the little tot go!"

The word also subtly carries a sense of cuteness and vulnerability. Calling someone a "tot" paints a picture of someone tiny, innocent, and endearing. You would never call a ten-year-old a tot — the word only works for very young children.

This meaning is used widely in both British and American English, and you will commonly see it in phrases like "tiny tots" — which is used to refer to young children as a group, for example in nursery programs, holiday events for young kids, or children's TV shows.
Meaning 2: A Small Measure of Spirits

The second meaning of "tot" is a small amount of a strong alcoholic drink, particularly spirits such as whisky, rum, or brandy. This meaning is especially common in British and Commonwealth English and may be less familiar to American speakers.

A tot in this sense is a modest, single serving of a spirit — not a large glass, but a short, small pour. If someone says, "I'll have a tot of rum before bed," they mean a small drink of rum, probably just enough to warm them up or help them wind down. It is the kind of drink you have in a quiet, considered way — not to get drunk, but to savour.

This meaning has a long history in naval and military culture, particularly in the British Royal Navy, where sailors were traditionally given a daily "tot" of rum as part of their rations. Even today, the phrase "tot of rum" carries a slightly old-fashioned, nautical flavour when used.

Though the two meanings seem unrelated on the surface, they are tied together by one consistent idea: a tot is always something small. A tot (child) is a tiny human. A tot (drink) is a tiny pour. The word essentially signals smallness no matter which sense you encounter it in.
How to Tell Which Meaning Is Intended

Context will almost always make it obvious. If someone says "the tots are napping," they mean children. If someone says "pour me a tot," they mean a drink. The two situations are so different that confusion between the two meanings is virtually impossible in real use.

"Tot" as a noun is an informal, everyday word in both of its meanings. It is warm, casual, and approachable. It is not slang, but it is not formal either. You would use it in conversation, in light writing, in journalism, or in fiction — but not in legal, medical, or academic documents.
Quick Mental Image to Remember Both Meanings

Think of "tot" as a word that always points to something small and dear — either a small, precious child, or a small, carefully poured drink. If you hold onto that core idea of smallness with a certain affection attached to it, you will always be in the right territory with this word.
14836:
"Totalitarian" is an adjective that describes a government, political system, or regime in which a single ruler, party, or group holds complete and absolute control over every single aspect of society — not just laws and government, but also the economy, education, the media, culture, religion, and even the private thoughts, beliefs, and personal lives of ordinary citizens. The word comes from the idea of "total" control — meaning there are no limits, no exceptions, and no part of life left untouched by the authority's reach.

If a government is totalitarian, it doesn't just rule the country — it tries to control and reshape everything and everyone inside it.
Breaking down what "total control" actually means

To understand this word properly, you need to feel the full weight of what "total control" looks like in practice. In a normal country, there are parts of life that the government simply doesn't get involved in. You can read what you like, believe what you like, talk to who you like, and criticize your leaders. The government controls some things, but your inner life — your mind, your faith, your personal relationships — largely belongs to you.

In a totalitarian system, that boundary doesn't exist. The government reaches into all of those spaces. Here is what that looks like across different areas of life:

Politics: Only one political party or leader is allowed to hold power. Opposition parties are banned, elections (if they exist at all) are rigged, and anyone who challenges the ruler is silenced, imprisoned, or worse. There is no peaceful transfer of power, no checks on authority.

Information and media: Newspapers, television, radio, books, and the internet (if available) are all controlled by the state. Citizens only receive information that the government approves. Inconvenient facts are hidden, rewritten, or denied. History itself is often rewritten to serve the regime.

Propaganda: A totalitarian government doesn't just silence opposing voices — it actively floods society with its own messaging. Citizens are constantly told what to think, what to feel, and who to blame. Schools teach children the regime's ideology from a very young age.

Surveillance: Citizens are watched. Secret police monitor people's conversations, movements, and associations. Citizens are often encouraged — or pressured — to report their neighbors, friends, and even family members for disloyalty. The goal is to make people feel that they are always being observed, so they police their own behavior out of fear.

Punishment: Dissent, criticism, or disobedience is met with severe consequences — arrest, torture, labor camps, execution, or the disappearance of loved ones. Fear is used as a tool of governance.

Economy: The state typically controls the production and distribution of goods and resources. People's livelihoods depend on the regime.

Ideology and loyalty: Citizens are not merely required to obey — they are required to believe, or at least to publicly perform belief. They must attend rallies, chant slogans, celebrate the leader, and demonstrate enthusiasm for the regime. Silence or neutrality can itself be seen as suspicious.

One of the most recognizable features of totalitarian regimes is what is called a "cult of personality" around the leader. The ruler is portrayed not as an ordinary human being who holds power, but as an almost god-like figure — a genius, a savior, the father of the nation, a being of almost supernatural wisdom and strength. His image appears everywhere: on posters, in schools, in offices. Citizens are expected to adore and revere him publicly. Criticizing him — even privately — is one of the most dangerous things a person can do.
How is it different from similar words?

Since you want a complete understanding, it's worth knowing how "totalitarian" differs from two similar words: authoritarian and dictatorial.

An authoritarian government is also one where a ruler or small group holds significant power and suppresses opposition. But authoritarian regimes mainly want to stay in political power — they don't necessarily care about controlling every part of your life. You might not be allowed to vote freely or criticize the president, but you can still run your private life relatively freely, practice your religion, watch your own entertainment, and so on.

A totalitarian system goes far beyond this. It isn't satisfied with merely controlling the government — it wants to transform all of society according to its ideology. It reaches into the economy, culture, art, family life, thought, and belief. The ambition is total.

A dictatorial system simply refers to rule by a dictator — one person with unlimited authority. Dictatorships can be totalitarian, but don't have to be. A dictator might rule ruthlessly but still leave large parts of everyday social life alone.

Think of it on a scale: all totalitarian regimes are authoritarian, but not all authoritarian regimes are totalitarian. Totalitarianism is the most extreme end of the scale.

The clearest historical examples help bring this to life:

Nazi Germany (1933–1945) under Adolf Hitler is considered one of the defining examples. The Nazi party controlled politics, media, culture, education, and the military, enforced a rigid racial ideology, used secret police (the Gestapo) to monitor citizens, and carried out the Holocaust — the systematic murder of six million Jews and millions of others.

The Soviet Union under Joseph Stalin (1924–1953) is another central example. Stalin's regime controlled the economy through collective farming and state ownership, ran a massive secret police apparatus (the NKVD), sent millions to brutal labor camps (the Gulag), conducted "purges" in which political rivals and perceived enemies were executed, and enforced Communist ideology throughout all of society.

North Korea today is widely considered the most totalitarian state currently in existence. The ruling Kim family is treated as almost divine. Citizens have virtually no access to outside information, movement is strictly controlled, and the state monitors every aspect of daily life.

Fascist Italy under Benito Mussolini is also an early example, and notably, it was in Italy in the 1920s that the word "totalitarian" was first used — actually by Mussolini himself, who used it proudly to describe his ambition for the state.

Understanding the opposite helps sharpen the definition. The opposite of a totalitarian system is a liberal democracy — a society where power is divided among different branches of government, citizens have protected rights and freedoms (speech, press, religion, assembly), elections are free and fair, opposition parties are allowed, and the rule of law applies to everyone, including those in power. In such systems, the government's reach is deliberately limited to protect individual liberty.
How the word is used (adjective in sentences)

Since "totalitarian" is an adjective, it typically modifies a noun:

  • "The citizens fled the totalitarian regime in search of freedom."
  • "She grew up under totalitarian rule and had never known a free press."
  • "The new law was criticized as a step toward totalitarian control."
  • "Totalitarian governments use fear and propaganda to maintain power."
  • "The party's totalitarian ambitions extended to controlling what art was allowed."

Common noun pairings you'll see: totalitarian regime, totalitarian state, totalitarian government, totalitarian rule, totalitarian system, totalitarian control, totalitarian ideology.
The key feeling of the word

If you want one sentence to carry the word in your mind forever, it's this:

A totalitarian system is one where the government's power has no limits — it controls not just the country, but every person in it, right down to what they are allowed to think and feel.

That is the heart of it. "Totalitarian" describes the most suffocating, all-consuming form of political control that human societies have ever produced.
14837:
When people say "a tote" or "a tote bag," they mean a large, open, sturdy bag with two handles that you carry things in.

Picture a simple, roomy bag — wide at the top, no complicated zippers or flaps closing it off, and two straps (handles) that are long enough to hang over your shoulder or be held in your hand. That's a tote.

What it looks like:

  • Open at the top (or lightly closed), so you can just drop things in
  • Two parallel handles, usually the same length
  • Rectangular or slightly tapered shape — wide and spacious
  • Made from cloth (canvas, cotton, jute), leather, nylon, or even plastic

Why people use it:
A tote is casual and practical. People bring them to grocery stores (instead of plastic bags), to the beach, to the gym, to a library, or just as an everyday carry bag. It holds a lot without being complicated.

Examples in sentences:

  • "She packed her lunch and water bottle in her tote."
  • "He brought a large canvas tote to carry his books."
  • "I always keep a tote bag in my car for shopping."

One important nuance: Unlike a handbag (which is more structured and formal) or a backpack (worn on your back), a tote is deliberately simple and unfussy. It's meant to be thrown over a shoulder and filled up without ceremony. Its charm is in that simplicity — no buckles, no complicated pockets, just a big open space.
A second meaning — a large storage container

In industrial and warehouse settings, a tote can also refer to a large, rigid plastic bin or box used to carry or store goods. Think of a sturdy plastic crate with handles on the sides, used to move inventory in a factory or store. These are also called tote bins or tote boxes.

Example:

  • "The workers stacked the totes on the shelves to organize the parts."

This meaning shares the same core idea as the bag: a container you use to carry or hold things.
A third meaning — "the tote" (betting, mainly British/Australian)

In British and Australian English, "the tote" (almost always said with "the") refers to a system of betting on horse races where all the money wagered is pooled together, and the winnings are shared among the people who bet correctly — after the organizer takes a small cut. It's short for totalisator (the machine/system that manages this).

Example:

  • "He placed his bet at the tote before the race started."

This meaning is quite specific — you'll mainly encounter it in the context of horse racing in Britain or Australia.

If you hear…It likely means…

If someone says "grab a tote" or "I love my tote," they almost certainly mean the bag. That is by far the most common use of this word in everyday life. The industrial container meaning appears in warehouses and logistics. The betting meaning is specific to horse racing in British and Australian English.

The thread connecting all three meanings is the same idea: a container or carrier — something that holds things and helps you move them. A tote is always a vessel for carrying.
14838:
To tote something means to carry it, usually with your hands, arms, or on your body — and almost always something physical and tangible. That's the heart of it.

But "tote" is not just a fancy synonym for "carry." It has a specific flavour that makes it distinct, and understanding that flavour is what truly makes the word yours.

"Carry" is a broad, neutral word. You can carry a conversation, carry hope, carry a tune — it works both literally and figuratively. It doesn't say much about effort or weight.

"Tote," on the other hand, is almost always literal and physical. And it quietly suggests one or more of the following:

  • The thing you're carrying has some weight or bulk to it — it's not a feather.
  • You're moving it a distance, not just picking it up and putting it back down.
  • You're carrying it on your person, close to your body — in your hands, over your shoulder, under your arm.
  • There's a sense of effort or personal burden — you are the one doing the work, with your own body.

So when someone says "She toted her bag to the market," the image is vivid: a real person, physically hauling something, getting it from one place to another themselves.

Tote is an informal, conversational word. You'd say it to a friend, read it in a novel, or hear it in casual speech. You wouldn't typically use it in a formal essay or a legal document.

It also carries a slightly vivid, down-to-earth quality. It paints a picture. It feels a little more colourful and specific than "carry." Writers often choose "tote" when they want the reader to actually see someone hauling something around.
What Kinds of Things Do You Tote?

You tote physical, tangible objects — things you can hold, lift, or strap on. Common examples include:

  • Bags, backpacks, suitcases, briefcases
  • Groceries, supplies, equipment, tools
  • Books, files, boxes
  • A baby or a child (carried on your body)
  • A gun (you'll often see "gun-toting" — meaning someone who goes around carrying a firearm)

Basically: if it's something with weight that you lug around with you, you can tote it.

Because "tote" is almost always physical, you generally don't tote abstract things. You wouldn't say "She toted her sadness everywhere she went" — that's where "carry" or "bear" would be used instead. Tote stays grounded in the real, physical world.

Here are the most natural ways "tote" is used:

Basic pattern — Subject + tote + object

  • He toted the heavy boxes up three flights of stairs.
  • She toted her laptop and notebooks to every class.

Tote around — carrying something from place to place, often repeatedly or habitually

  • He always totes a notebook around wherever he goes.
  • Why are you toting those groceries around in this heat?

Tote along — bringing something with you on a trip or outing

  • Don't forget to tote along a water bottle.
  • She toted her camera along on the hike.

-toting (as a suffix in descriptions) — used to describe someone who habitually carries a particular thing

  • gun-toting cowboys (cowboys who go around carrying guns)
  • briefcase-toting executives (executives always seen with briefcases)

One subtle but important nuance: "tote" often implies that the carrying is something you do regularly or as a matter of habit, or at least that you're doing it deliberately, with intent — you're not just holding something for a second. You're going places with it, or you make a habit of having it on you.

"She totes her sketchbook everywhere" — she always has it, she brings it along constantly. That's the natural home of this word.

What it meansTo carry something physical, usually with effort, on your body or in your hands
Compared to "carry"More vivid, more physical, implies weight/bulk and some distance or habit
ToneInformal, conversational, everyday
Works withPhysical objects (bags, boxes, guns, babies, gear, groceries)
Doesn't work withAbstract things (emotions, ideas, metaphors)
Common add-onstote around, tote along, -toting
A Few Sentences to Cement It

• Every morning, he totes a massive thermos of coffee to the office.
  • The porters toted luggage up the steep mountain path for the tourists.
  • She toted her young son on her hip as she moved through the crowded market.
  • He's always toting some new gadget around — today it was a drone.
  • The gun-toting bandits rode into town at dusk.

After reading this, you know not just what "tote" means, but when to use it, how it feels, and what makes it different from simpler alternatives. That's true ownership of a word.
14839:
A totem is a natural entity — most often an animal, but sometimes a plant, a natural force (like thunder or wind), or even an object — that a group of people (or sometimes an individual) regards as having a deep, sacred spiritual bond with them.

The totem is not just a symbol on paper. People who belong to a totem believe they share a living, meaningful relationship with that entity. They might see it as their ancestor, their protector, their spiritual guide, or the very source of their identity.

Think of it this way: if your clan's totem is the eagle, you don't just like eagles or think they're cool. You believe your people are connected to eagles in a profound, almost blood-like way — that the eagle watches over you, that you carry the eagle's spirit, and that the eagle in some sense is your people.

Totemism — the belief system built around totems — is ancient and has appeared across many cultures: Indigenous peoples of North America, Aboriginal Australians, tribes in West Africa, Siberian peoples, and many others. It is not tied to one religion or one part of the world. It is a deeply human way of making sense of the relationship between people and the natural world.

There are two main kinds of totems:

1. Clan or Tribal Totems (the most common kind)

These belong to an entire group — a family, a clan, or a tribe. Every member of that group shares the same totem. The totem:

  • Gives the group its identity and name (e.g., "the Bear Clan")
  • Acts as a protector of the whole group
  • Is treated with great respect, sometimes even reverence

In many cultures, members of a clan are forbidden from harming, hunting, or eating their totem animal. To harm the totem is to harm yourself and your people. This rule is called a taboo.

Members of the same totem group also often cannot marry each other. They are considered spiritual kin — almost like siblings — even if they share no blood relation.

2. Individual Totems

Some cultures also have the concept of a personal totem — a spirit animal or entity that belongs specifically to one person. This is your own spiritual guardian, a being that guides you through life, lends you its qualities (courage, wisdom, cunning), and protects you personally. In some traditions, a person discovers their individual totem through a ceremony, a dream, a vision, or a solitary journey into nature.

A totem serves several important roles at once:

  • Identity: It tells you who you are and where you belong. "I am of the Wolf Clan."
  • Protection: The totem is believed to watch over and shield its group.
  • Moral guidance: The qualities of the totem animal — say, the patience of a turtle or the strength of a bear — are qualities the group strives to embody.
  • Ancestry: In many traditions, the totem is seen as a common ancestor. The Bear Clan might believe they literally descended from bears, or that a bear-spirit was the founding ancestor of their line.
  • Sacred boundary: Rules around the totem (don't kill it, don't eat it, don't disrespect it) create a code of behavior that holds the group together.

You may have heard of totem poles. These are tall, carved wooden structures made by Indigenous peoples of the Pacific Northwest Coast of North America (groups like the Haida, Tlingit, and Tsimshian). They are one of the most famous physical expressions of totemism.

A totem pole is stacked with carved figures — animals, humans, supernatural beings — that tell a story. Each figure represents a totem, an ancestor, a legend, or an important event in a family or clan's history. They are not objects of worship; rather, they are more like illustrated records — a visual history carved in wood, displayed proudly for the community and visitors to read.
The Word in Everyday Modern Usage

Today, the word "totem" has spilled beyond its original cultural and spiritual context into everyday language. People now use it more loosely to mean:

Any object, symbol, or figure that represents something deeply and powerfully.

For example:

  • "The bald eagle is a totem of American identity." (Here it means a powerful symbol.)
  • "The old oak tree became a totem for the village — something everyone rallied around."
  • A luxury car or a status symbol might be called a "status totem" — an object people cling to as a sign of who they are.

In the 2010 film Inception, each character carries a personal "totem" — a small object they use to tell whether they are in reality or a dream. This is a creative use of the word, drawing on its idea of a deeply personal, identity-defining object.

AspectWhat it means

A totem is about belonging and connection. It answers the question: What in the natural world are we spiritually tied to? That tie shapes a group's name, its rules, its pride, its history, and its relationship with the world around it. The totem is not just a logo or a mascot — in the cultures where it is truly alive, it is as real and as important as family.

In its broadest, modern sense, a totem is simply something — an object, a symbol, a figure — that carries deep meaning for a person or a group, something they identify with so strongly that it becomes a stand-in for who they are.
14840:
A totem pole is a tall, carved wooden post created by certain Indigenous (Native) peoples of the Pacific Northwest Coast of North America. Think of it as a wooden story-book, standing upright, where instead of words, the stories are told through carved figures stacked one on top of another — animals, humans, mythological creatures, and spirit beings.

These poles can be enormous. Some stand as tall as a three- or four-story building.

A totem pole is usually made from a single large tree trunk — most commonly red cedar, because cedar is both strong and resistant to decay. The carver (an artist with great skill and deep cultural knowledge) carves directly into the wood, creating figures that seem to emerge from the pole itself. The finished pole is then painted in bold, striking colours — typically black, red, and blue-green — using a distinct artistic style unique to these cultures.

The figures on a totem pole are not random. Each one has a specific identity and meaning. Common figures include:

  • Animals — eagles, ravens, bears, beavers, wolves, killer whales, frogs, and salmon
  • Human ancestors — real or legendary people from the family's history
  • Supernatural beings — mythological creatures from the culture's traditions

These figures are stacked vertically, one above the other, from the bottom of the pole to the very top.

Each figure on a totem pole represents a totem — a spiritual being, animal, or ancestor that is deeply connected to a particular family, clan, or lineage (a line of ancestors). Think of a totem as a family's spiritual symbol or emblem, similar in spirit to a family crest in European tradition, but far richer in meaning.

Together, the figures on a totem pole tell a story. That story might be about:

  • The history of a family or clan — who they are, where they come from, what great events shaped them
  • A legend or myth — a famous story from their cultural tradition
  • A supernatural encounter — when an ancestor met a spirit being and formed a bond with it
  • The achievements or status of a person or family

Reading a totem pole is like reading a visual language. To fully understand it, you need to know the culture's stories, symbols, and traditions.

Totem poles are not all the same — they serve several different purposes:

  1. Memorial poles — Erected to honour and remember a great chief or important person who has died. They keep that person's legacy alive.
  2. House poles — These are carved posts built into the structure of a traditional home. They might frame the doorway or stand inside the house. They declare the identity and status of the family who lives there.
  3. Mortuary poles — A special type of pole that actually holds the remains (ashes or bones) of a deceased person inside a compartment carved into the top.
  4. Shame poles — Erected to publicly embarrass someone who has done wrong — for example, someone who broke a promise, refused to repay a debt, or acted dishonourably. This was a powerful social tool, because public shame carried great weight in these communities. Interestingly, the offending person's image is often carved upside down on the pole.
  5. Welcome poles — Placed near a shoreline or village entrance to greet visitors and travellers arriving by canoe.

Totem poles are made by the Indigenous peoples of the Northwest Coast, a region stretching from Alaska in the north, through British Columbia (Canada), and down into parts of Washington State and Oregon (USA). These include nations such as the Haida, Tlingit, Tsimshian, Kwakwaka'wakw (Kwakiutl), Nuu-chah-nulth, and several others.

Each nation has its own artistic style, symbols, and traditions, so totem poles from different groups look distinct from one another if you know what to look for.

The craft of carving totem poles is a serious, respected art form, passed down through generations. A totem pole carver is not just an artist — they are a keeper of cultural knowledge.
A Very Important Misconception to Clear Up

Many people assume totem poles are religious idols that people worship or pray to. This is incorrect. Totem poles are not objects of worship. They are better understood as monuments or records — like a carved, three-dimensional history book or a prestigious family coat of arms. They command respect, but they are not prayed to.

Beyond its literal meaning, the phrase totem pole is widely used in everyday English as a figure of speech to describe a hierarchy — a system where people or things are ranked from most powerful to least powerful.

The most common expression is:

"Low man on the totem pole"

This means someone who is at the bottom of a hierarchy — the least important, least experienced, or least powerful person in a group or organisation. For example: "As the newest employee, I was the low man on the totem pole and got all the least desirable tasks."

(Interestingly, in many real totem poles, the bottom figure is actually the most important one — so this idiom is somewhat ironic from a cultural accuracy standpoint. But the figurative meaning in everyday English is well-established and widely understood.)

A totem pole is a tall carved wooden post made by Indigenous peoples of the Pacific Northwest Coast of North America, covered in stacked figures of animals, ancestors, and supernatural beings. Each pole tells a story — about a family's history, a cultural legend, or a person's legacy. They serve various purposes: honouring the dead, declaring family identity, welcoming guests, or even publicly shaming wrongdoers. They are not objects of worship but rather powerful cultural records and artistic achievements. In everyday English, the term is also used figuratively to describe where someone stands in a hierarchy.
14841: Something is "totemic" when it functions like a sacred tribal symbol — it stands for something much larger than itself, is deeply tied to a group's identity, and is treated with a kind of reverence that goes beyond rational evaluation.
Start here: what is a totem?

Before the adjective makes sense, you need to understand the noun it comes from.

In many indigenous cultures around the world, a totem is an animal, plant, or object that a clan or tribe adopts as their sacred emblem. It is not merely a logo or a mascot. The totem is believed to have a spiritual bond with the group — it may represent their ancestors, their guardian spirit, or the deepest values of their community. Tribe members don't just admire the totem; they feel constituted by it. They may refuse to kill or eat the totemic animal. They carve its image onto poles and walls. They treat it with the kind of seriousness most people reserve for holy objects.

So a totem is not just important. It is sacred. It is the living symbol of a group's soul.

When you call something "totemic," you are saying it works like a totem. Specifically, it means the thing:

  • Has become a powerful, almost sacred symbol of a group, movement, culture, or era
  • Represents something far larger and deeper than what it literally is
  • Is treated with reverence — people feel strongly attached to it on an almost emotional or spiritual level
  • Is so tied to a group's identity that questioning it can feel like an attack on the group itself

The single most important idea is this: a totemic thing has transcended its literal function. It no longer matters only for what it actually is — it matters for what it represents.

Today, "totemic" is used far beyond the world of tribes and rituals. It appears in journalism, literature, political writing, and intellectual conversation to describe anything that has taken on profound symbolic weight within a group or culture.

A few examples will make this click:

"Nelson Mandela was a totemic figure of the anti-apartheid struggle."
He wasn't just one man in prison. To millions of people, he embodied the entire struggle — the suffering, the hope, the moral force, the resistance. He carried meaning that went far beyond one individual's biography.

"The iPhone became a totemic object of the early 21st century."
It wasn't just a phone. It came to represent an entire era of technological transformation, design philosophy, and modern culture. People lined up for it not just for its features but because of what owning one meant.

"For many conservatives, the Second Amendment has become totemic."
This means it has moved beyond being a legal provision. For a large group of people, it now symbolizes their identity, their values, and their way of life — and is defended with the intensity people normally reserve for sacred things.

"The Che Guevara photograph is totemic for leftist movements worldwide."
That single image no longer functions as just a portrait. It carries the weight of revolution, idealism, and resistance. People wear it on t-shirts not because they know his biography but because of what the image stands for.

In each case, notice the pattern: the thing (a man, a phone, a law, an image) has been elevated by a group into something that represents their collective identity, values, and beliefs. That is what "totemic" captures.

This is where the word gets genuinely sophisticated. When a writer describes something as "totemic," they are often also quietly pointing to something about how people relate to it — and that relationship is not always fully rational.

Just as a tribe does not calmly debate the merits of their totem, people tend not to evaluate totemic symbols with cool detachment. They feel them. A totemic symbol becomes so fused with group identity that criticism of the symbol feels like criticism of the group. This is why totemic objects, figures, and ideas are so fiercely defended — even when rational arguments against them exist.

So when a writer calls a political idea "totemic" for a certain party, or calls a historical figure "totemic" for a movement, there is often a subtle suggestion that the symbol has become somewhat unquestionable within the group — accepted on faith and identity rather than pure reason. The word can be used neutrally, admiringly, or critically, depending on context, but this psychological undercurrent is almost always present.
How it differs from similar words

"Totemic" is frequently confused with words like iconic, symbolic, legendary, or emblematic. Here is why it is stronger and more specific than all of them:

Something iconic is simply very famous and widely recognized. Something symbolic just represents something else. Something legendary is famous and celebrated through stories. But something totemic does all of this and carries the additional weight of group identity, quasi-sacred status, and the kind of emotional intensity that tribes feel toward their sacred emblems. It implies a depth of attachment that the other words do not.

Think of it this way: every totemic thing is iconic, but not every iconic thing is totemic. The Eiffel Tower is iconic. The French flag, to the French people, is closer to totemic.

"Totemic" is a formal, intellectually charged word. You will encounter it in serious journalism, academic writing, essays, and literary criticism. It is almost never used in casual conversation. When a writer reaches for "totemic" instead of "iconic" or "important," they are making a deliberate, precise choice — they want to convey that something has achieved a mythic symbolic power, not just fame or significance.

Totemic describes something that functions like a sacred tribal totem: it is a powerful symbol deeply bound to the identity and values of a group, treated with near-reverence, and carrying meaning far greater than its literal form. Whether applied to a person, object, image, or idea, calling something "totemic" says: this thing has become almost sacred to a group — it carries the weight of who they are, what they believe, and what they stand for. The word also carries a quiet psychological observation: that people relate to totemic things with emotional intensity rather than detached analysis, which is precisely what makes such symbols so powerful — and so hard to question.
14842:
To totter means to move or stand in an unsteady, shaky way — as if you are about to lose your balance and fall at any moment. It is not a fast, dramatic fall. It is that slow, wobbly, uncertain moment before a possible fall, where something or someone is struggling to stay upright but clearly not doing a great job of it.

Think of a toddler taking their very first steps. They lean too far left, then too far right, their little legs barely cooperating, their whole body swaying. That is tottering. They haven't fallen yet, but it looks like they might at any second.

The word carries a very specific feeling. It is not just about being unsteady in a frozen, still way. It implies movement — either the movement of walking, or the movement of swaying and rocking back and forth. The instability is active, not passive. Something is in motion, and that motion is fragile and uncertain.

It also implies slowness. You wouldn't use "totter" to describe someone who trips and falls suddenly. It describes a prolonged, shaky, wobbling state.

People

This is the most common use. A person totters when they walk or stand without proper balance or steadiness.

  • A very old person with weak legs might totter as they walk across a room.
  • Someone wearing very high heels on uneven ground might totter with each step.
  • A sick person who is dizzy might totter when they try to get out of bed.
  • A person who has had too much to drink might totter down the street.

In all these cases, the person is moving, but every step looks like it could be their last before they tumble over.

Objects

Objects that sway or wobble as if about to fall can also totter.

  • A tall pile of books stacked carelessly on a desk might totter when someone bumps the table.
  • An old, rotting fence post might totter in the wind.
  • A child's tower of building blocks totters before it collapses.

Here, "totter" is perfect because it captures that suspenseful moment — the thing hasn't fallen yet, but it is clearly on the edge.

"Totter" is also used in a powerful figurative sense to describe systems, institutions, governments, or organisations that are on the verge of collapse or failure. Just as a person totters before they fall, a powerful structure can "totter" before it crumbles.

  • "The government is tottering under the weight of scandal after scandal."
  • "The company's finances were so bad that the entire business was tottering on the edge of bankruptcy."
  • "The old empire, once mighty, began to totter as rebellions spread across its borders."

In this figurative sense, "totter" tells you that collapse has not happened yet, but it is very close and very likely. It gives a sense of things unravelling slowly but surely.
The Emotional Colour of the Word

"Totter" is not a neutral word. It often carries a feeling of vulnerability, fragility, and sympathy. When we say a person totters, we feel slightly sorry for them — they are struggling. When we say a great institution totters, there is often a sense of sadness or drama, the sense of something once-great now failing.

It can also carry a sense of suspense — will it fall or won't it?
How It Compares to Similar Words

Understanding how "totter" sits among similar words will sharpen your feel for it:

Stagger — This is more dramatic and erratic. Someone who staggers lurches heavily from side to side, often because of a sudden impact, extreme exhaustion, or drunkenness. Staggering is wilder and more violent-looking than tottering. An injured boxer staggers; a frail grandmother totters.

Teeter — This focuses on the balance point — the moment of being exactly between falling and not falling, like a seesaw paused in the middle. You teeter on the edge of something. Totter is more about the overall unsteady movement, while teeter is about that knife-edge, tipping-point moment.

Wobble — This describes the back-and-forth or side-to-side motion itself. A wobble can be small and harmless (a plate wobbling on a table). Totter always carries the additional sense of potential collapse or falling. Something that totters is also wobbling, but something that wobbles isn't necessarily in danger of falling.

Stumble — This is about catching your foot or losing your footing briefly, often resulting in a near-fall. It is a specific, momentary event. Totter describes an ongoing unsteady state, not a single moment.
Quick Mental Image to Remember It Forever

Picture a very old, thin candle sitting in a candleholder. It has been burning for hours. It is now barely held upright, leaning and swaying slightly in the breeze from an open window. It hasn't fallen yet. But you're watching it nervously, knowing it could tip over any second.

That candle is tottering.

Whenever you see or imagine that image — slow, uncertain, fragile, on the edge — that is exactly what "totter" means, whether applied to a person walking, an object swaying, or a great institution beginning to fail.
14843:
"Touch base" means to make brief contact with someone — usually just to check in, share a quick update, or stay connected. It's not a deep conversation. It's not a formal meeting. It's simply saying: "Hey, let's talk briefly so we're both on the same page."

Think of it like this: imagine you and a friend are working on a group project separately. At the end of the day, one of you says, "Let me touch base with you tomorrow morning." That just means: "Let's have a quick chat tomorrow to see where things stand."
Where Did This Phrase Come From?

The phrase comes from baseball, the American sport.

In baseball, a runner must physically touch each base (first base, second base, third base, and home plate) as they run around the field. If they miss a base — even by an inch — they're called out. Touching the base is a necessary, brief, but important action that keeps everything in order.

Over time, people borrowed this idea and applied it to communication. Just like a runner briefly touches a base before moving on, you "touch base" with a person — make brief contact — before continuing with your work or life.
The Core Idea Behind the Phrase

There are three key things that define "touch base":

1. It's brief. This is not a long, detailed meeting. It's a quick check-in — maybe five minutes, or even just a short email or phone call.

2. It's about staying connected or informed. The goal is simply to make sure both people know what's going on. It prevents misunderstandings and keeps communication alive.

3. It often happens between people who already know each other. You don't usually "touch base" with a complete stranger. It's used between colleagues, teammates, managers and employees, friends, or business partners.
How to Use It in a Sentence

The phrase is almost always used with these structures:

  • "Let's touch base" → a suggestion to check in
  • "I wanted to touch base with you" → saying you reached out to check in
  • "Touch base with [someone]" → telling someone to check in with another person
  • "We touched base" → saying the check-in already happened

Here are real-life examples across different situations:

At work:

"I'll touch base with you after the meeting to share what was discussed."

"Can we touch base on Friday? I want to make sure the project is on track."

Between a manager and employee:

"My manager asked me to touch base with the client before sending the proposal."

In casual life:

"I haven't spoken to Jake in a while. I should touch base with him."

In an email subject line:

Subject: Touching Base — Quick Update

"Touch base" lives comfortably in both professional and casual settings, which makes it very versatile.

  • In the workplace, it's used constantly in emails, meetings, and Slack messages. It sounds professional without being stiff or overly formal.
  • Among friends or family, it's slightly less common, but still perfectly natural to say, "Let's touch base this week."

It is not rude, not too formal, and not too casual — it sits right in the middle, which is exactly why it became so popular in business communication.
What It Does NOT Mean (Avoid These Mistakes)

Since you're a learner, it helps to know what this phrase does not mean:

  • ❌ It does not mean a long, serious discussion or a full meeting.
  • ❌ It does not mean physically touching something (despite the word "touch").
  • ❌ It does not mean solving a problem — it's just a check-in, not a solution session.
  • ❌ It does not suggest anything is wrong. Saying "let's touch base" is neutral and routine — it's not a warning sign or a serious summons.

You'll often hear or read slightly different forms of the same idea:

  • "Circle back" — very similar; means to return to a topic or person later.
  • "Check in" — almost identical in meaning; slightly more casual than "touch base."
  • "Catch up" — a bit warmer; often implies talking about more than just work.
  • "Loop in" — means to include someone in a conversation or email chain.
  • "Reconnect" — similar, but often used when more time has passed without contact.

Among all of these, "touch base" is arguably the most common in professional (especially corporate) environments.

"Touch base" is so widely used in business and office culture that some people consider it a corporate buzzword — meaning it's used so often that it can start to sound robotic or hollow. In very creative or informal workplaces, some people prefer saying "let's catch up" or simply "let's talk" instead.

That said, it's completely correct and widely understood everywhere, so using it will never be wrong — it's simply a matter of style.

"Touch base" means to briefly contact or check in with someone, usually to share a quick update or stay informed — nothing more, nothing less.

Master that idea, and you've fully understood the phrase.
14844: "Touchy" means easily upset or sensitive in a way that requires careful handling. Think of it like a bruise on your skin — even a light touch causes pain. A touchy person, or a touchy subject, is the same: even a small or innocent remark can cause a big reaction.

The word "touchy" is used in two closely related ways:

1. To describe a person

When you call a person touchy, you mean they get offended, upset, or irritated very easily — often over things that most people would not mind at all. The reaction they show feels bigger than the situation deserves.

  • "Don't joke about his cooking. He's very touchy about it."
  • "She gets touchy whenever someone mentions her age."
  • "Why are you so touchy today? I only asked a simple question."

A touchy person doesn't necessarily stay angry for a long time. The word is more about how quickly and easily they get triggered, not how long the feeling lasts.

2. To describe a subject, topic, or situation

When a topic or situation is touchy, it means it is sensitive and delicate — the kind of thing where you have to choose your words very carefully, because it can easily upset people or cause arguments.

  • "Money is a touchy subject in their family."
  • "The question of religion is always a touchy topic at the dinner table."
  • "The negotiations are in a touchy situation right now — one wrong move could ruin everything."

Notice that in this second use, it's not about one particular person being overly sensitive. It's about the nature of the topic itself — it carries enough emotional weight that most people would feel uncomfortable or defensive about it.
The Key Feeling Behind the Word

Whether "touchy" describes a person or a topic, there is always an underlying fragility involved. Something could go wrong very easily. You feel the need to tread lightly — to be careful, gentle, and measured.

This is why people say things like:

  • "I have to be careful how I bring this up — it's a touchy area."
  • "He's touchy today, so don't say anything that could be taken the wrong way."

"Touchy" carries a mildly negative connotation when describing a person. It subtly suggests that the person is being more sensitive than the situation really calls for — that they are overreacting a little. It's not a harsh insult, but it does signal mild frustration or impatience with someone's oversensitivity.

Compare these two sentences:

  • "She is sensitive." → This sounds neutral or even sympathetic.
  • "She is touchy." → This hints that her sensitivity is slightly excessive or inconvenient for others.

When describing a topic or situation, however, "touchy" is more neutral and descriptive. It simply warns you that care is needed, without judging anyone.

• Touchy about something: "He's touchy about his weight." (sensitive regarding a specific thing)
  • A touchy subject / topic / issue / area: "That's a touchy subject in our office."
  • A touchy situation: "We're in a touchy situation with our landlord."
  • Don't be so touchy: A direct way of telling someone they are overreacting to something.

• Sensitive can be a compliment — a sensitive person understands others' feelings well. "Touchy" is almost never a compliment.
  • Irritable means someone is in a bad mood and gets annoyed easily right now. "Touchy" describes more of a recurring tendency or trait, often tied to a specific subject.
  • Delicate (when describing a situation) is more formal and serious. "Touchy" is more conversational and informal.
  • Temperamental means someone's mood shifts unpredictably. "Touchy" is more specifically about being quick to take offense.

UseWhat it means

In short: if a person is touchy, they get offended or upset far too easily. If a subject or situation is touchy, it is emotionally sensitive and must be handled with care. In both cases, the word signals: proceed carefully, because something could go wrong very easily here.
14845:
"Touché" is what you say when someone makes a point so sharp, so well-aimed, or so clever in a conversation that you have to admit — right there and then — that they got you. It's a gracious, sporting acknowledgment that the other person scored a hit in a battle of words or ideas.

Think of it as a concise way of saying: "Okay. You got me there. That was a good one."

When you say "touché," you're making a very specific admission. You're saying that the other person's point effectively countered what you said, or caught you in a contradiction or a flaw in your thinking, or was simply so witty and well-placed that you can't honestly argue back.

Importantly, you are not surrendering the entire argument or saying the other person is right about everything. You're conceding just that one exchange — acknowledging that in this particular moment, they landed a clean, undeniable hit on you.
The Tone and Spirit Behind It

This is crucial: "touché" is almost never said in anger, bitterness, or resentment. It has a light, good-natured, even playful quality. There's a kind of sportsmanship in it — the way a chess player might smile and nod at a brilliant move that boxed them in.

When you say it, you're signaling that you're a good sport who can appreciate cleverness even when it's directed at you, and that you find the exchange fun rather than threatening. This is why the word tends to appear in witty banter, friendly debates, and spirited arguments between people who respect each other — not in bitter, hostile fights.

Being caught in a contradiction:

You: "You're always late!"
Friend: "You're the one who told me last week that punctuality is overrated."
You: "...Touché."

Your friend used your own words against you. You literally argued that punctuality doesn't matter, so you can't now complain about lateness without looking hypocritical. You've been fairly caught, and you admit it.

A sharp, witty comeback:

A: "You never exercise."
B: "I just walked away from this conversation, didn't I?"
A: "Touché."

B's joke worked as a genuine counter. It was clever, it landed, and A has to admit that.

Catching a double standard:

A: "You spend way too much money."
B: "You bought three coffees today."
A: "Touché."

A was criticizing B, but B pointed out that A does the very same thing. That's a fair and effective counter, and A admits it.

Turning your words around on you:

A: "You always have an excuse for everything."
B: "And you always have a complaint for everything."
A: "...Touché."

B flipped A's own criticism right back on them, fairly and neatly. It works, and A knows it.

Use "touché" when someone makes a clever comeback in a playful or competitive exchange, catches a genuine flaw in your argument, uses your own logic or words back against you, points out that you're being hypocritical, or makes an observation so sharp and accurate that you genuinely have nothing to say. The key ingredients are: a verbal exchange, a point that truly lands against you, and your willingness to acknowledge it with grace.

Don't use "touché" in a deeply serious or emotional argument — it can come across as flippant or dismissive, as though you're not taking the matter seriously. Don't use it just because someone states a fact you already knew; the point has to be sharp, surprising, or cleverly constructed. Don't use it simply because someone disagrees with you — disagreement alone isn't a hit, the counter has to genuinely work. It's also a conversational expression, not suited for formal writing.

Like many expressions, "touché" can be used sarcastically. If someone makes a point that wasn't clever at all, you might say "touché" in a slow, exaggerated, mocking way to signal that you're completely unimpressed. For example:

A: "Well, maybe you're the problem!"
B: (rolls eyes) "...Touché."

Here, B is using "touché" ironically — the comeback was weak, not sharp, and B is making that obvious through tone and delivery. Context always makes this version clear.
What It Reveals About the Person Who Says It

One last thing worth knowing: saying "touché" correctly — and genuinely meaning it — reflects well on you. It means you're sharp enough to recognize when someone has beaten you at your own game, and honest enough to say so out loud rather than awkwardly deflecting. People who use it well come across as witty, confident, gracious, and secure — not people who need to win every single point in every single exchange.
14846:
A tough cookie is a person who is mentally and emotionally strong. When someone faces difficult situations — pain, hardship, failure, pressure, or criticism — and does not break down, give up, or get easily hurt, we call them a tough cookie.

Think of it simply: a tough cookie is someone who is hard to crack.

The image comes from a literal cookie (the baked snack). Most cookies are soft and crumble easily. But a tough cookie is hard — if you try to break it, it resists.

People applied this to human personality: just like a hard cookie is difficult to break apart, a tough cookie person is difficult to break down emotionally or mentally.

The word "cookie" has been used informally in English for a long time to refer to a person, especially in American English — for example, "a smart cookie" (a clever person) or "a tough cookie." The use of "tough cookie" became widespread in American English through the 20th century.
The Core Idea: What Makes Someone a "Tough Cookie"?

A tough cookie typically shows some or all of these qualities:

  • Resilience — they bounce back from setbacks instead of staying down
  • Mental strength — they don't collapse under pressure or stress
  • Emotional toughness — criticism, insults, or harsh words don't easily wound them
  • Determination — they keep going when things get hard
  • Self-reliance — they don't need others to rescue or comfort them constantly
  • Composure — they stay calm and in control in tough situations

The key point is that the strength is internal — it lives inside the person, not in their muscles or physical size.
Is It a Compliment or an Insult?

Almost always a compliment. When someone calls you a tough cookie, they are usually praising your strength and resilience. They are saying: "You're impressive. You've been through a lot, but you're still standing."

However, in rare situations, it can carry a slightly different tone.
